rmt-2005-power-01.title: Use the ray and the product
rmt-2005-power-01.body:
The distance from $(-6,8)$ to the origin is $10$, so the inversion lies on the same ray at distance $\frac{25}{10}=2.5$ from the origin. The unit vector toward $(-6,8)$ is $(-0.6,0.8)$, so $P'=2.5(-0.6,0.8)=(-1.5,2)$.

**Answer: $(-1.5,2)$**

rmt-2005-power-02.title: Use the ray and the product
rmt-2005-power-02.body:
The center is $(4,9)$ and $r^2=10$. The vector from the center to $(11,10)$ is $(7,1)$, of length squared $50$. The inversion is on the same ray at distance $\frac{10}{\sqrt{50}}$, i.e. $\frac{r^2}{50}=\frac15$ times the vector: $(4,9)+\frac15(7,1)=(5.4,9.2)$.

**Answer: $(5.4,9.2)$**

rmt-2005-power-03.title: Scale the vector
rmt-2005-power-03.body:
Let $\vec v=(x-x_0,y-y_0)$ and $d^2=|\vec v|^2=(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2$ (so $(x,y)\ne(x_0,y_0)$). The inversion $P'$ lies on the ray from the center through $P$, so $P'-C=\lambda\vec v$ with $\lambda>0$, and $|P'-C|=\lambda d$. The condition $d\cdot\lambda d=r^2$ gives $\lambda=\frac{r^2}{d^2}$. Hence $P'=\left(x_0+\frac{r^2(x-x_0)}{d^2},\,y_0+\frac{r^2(y-y_0)}{d^2}\right)$.

**Answer: as above (this reproduces Problems 1 and 2)**

rmt-2005-power-04a.title: Check the conditions
rmt-2005-power-04a.body: Note $P'\ne C$ (it is at distance $r^2/CP>0$), so its inversion is defined; call it $P''$. The point $P''$ lies on line $CP'$, which is line $CP$, on the ray $CP'$, which is ray $CP$; and $CP''=\frac{r^2}{CP'}=\frac{r^2}{r^2/CP}=CP$. A point on ray $CP$ at distance $CP$ from $C$ is $P$ itself. So $P''=P$. ∎

rmt-2005-power-04b.title: Use the product
rmt-2005-power-04b.body: If $P=P'$, then $CP=CP'$, so $(CP)^2=(CP)(CP')=r^2$. Distances are positive, so $CP=r$ and $P$ lies on $\bigcirc C$. ∎

rmt-2005-power-05.title: Similar right triangles
rmt-2005-power-05.body:
By symmetry in line $CP$ (which is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$), the tangents at $A$ and $B$ meet at a point $Y$ on line $CP$, on the same side of $C$ as $P$ (the tangents at $A$ and $B$ meet beyond chord $AB$), so $C$ is not between $P$ and $Y$.

In triangles $CPA$ and $CAY$: $\angle CPA=90^\circ$ (as $AB\perp CP$) and $\angle CAY=90^\circ$ (tangent is perpendicular to radius), and they share the angle at $C$. So the triangles are similar, giving $\frac{CP}{CA}=\frac{CA}{CY}$, i.e. $(CP)(CY)=CA^2=r^2$. Therefore $Y$ satisfies all three conditions, so $Y=P'$. ∎

rmt-2005-power-06a.title: Distances map to reciprocal distances
rmt-2005-power-06a.body:
Points of the segment at distance $d$ from $C$ map to the point at distance $\frac{r^2}d$ from $C$ on the same ray, and the map $d\mapsto\frac{r^2}d$ is continuous and decreasing.

**Case 1: $C$ is not on segment $AB$.** All points lie on one ray from $C$, with $d$ ranging over $[CA,CB]$ (say $CA\le CB$). Their images fill the interval of distances $\left[\frac{r^2}{CB},\frac{r^2}{CA}\right]$ on that ray, i.e. the segment $A'B'$.

**Case 2: $C$ is between $A$ and $B$.** The segment is the union of $CA$ and $CB$ (without $C$). On the ray toward $A$, distances $d\in(0,CA]$ map to distances $\left[\frac{r^2}{CA},\infty\right)$, a ray starting at $A'$ and going away from $C$. Likewise on the $B$ side. So the image is the line $AB$ minus the open segment $A'B'$ (which contains $C$).

**Answer: as stated above**

rmt-2005-power-06b.title: Rays map to themselves
rmt-2005-power-06b.body:
A point of the line at distance $d>0$ from $C$ goes to the point on the same ray at distance $\frac{r^2}d$. So each of the two open rays from $C$ goes into itself, and since $d\mapsto\frac{r^2}d$ takes all positive values exactly once, each open ray is mapped onto itself. Hence the image is the same line with $C$ removed.

**Answer: the line itself (without $C$)**

rmt-2005-power-07a.title: On the positive x-axis
rmt-2005-power-07a.body:
The point $(d,0)$ is on the positive $x$-axis at distance $d$ from the origin, so its inversion is on the positive $x$-axis at distance $\frac{r^2}d$, i.e. $\left(\frac{r^2}d,0\right)$.

**Answer: $\left(\frac{r^2}d,0\right)$**

rmt-2005-power-07b.title: Distance to infinity
rmt-2005-power-07b.body:
The distance from $(d,y)$ to the origin is $\sqrt{d^2+y^2}\to\infty$ as $y\to\pm\infty$, so the inversion lies at distance $\frac{r^2}{\sqrt{d^2+y^2}}\to0$ from the origin. Thus the inversion approaches $(0,0)$ (from the upper right or lower right).

**Answer: it approaches $(0,0)$**

rmt-2005-power-07c.title: Use coordinates
rmt-2005-power-07c.body:
By Problem 3 the inversion of $(d,y)$ is $(X,Y)=\left(\frac{r^2d}{d^2+y^2},\frac{r^2y}{d^2+y^2}\right)$. Then $X^2+Y^2=\frac{r^4(d^2+y^2)}{(d^2+y^2)^2}=\frac{r^4}{d^2+y^2}$ and $\frac{r^2}{d}X=\frac{r^4}{d^2+y^2}$. So $X^2+Y^2=\frac{r^2}{d}X$, i.e. $\left(X-\frac{r^2}{2d}\right)^2+Y^2=\left(\frac{r^2}{2d}\right)^2$: the image lies on the circle with center $\left(\frac{r^2}{2d},0\right)$ and radius $\frac{r^2}{2d}$.

Conversely, let $(X,Y)\ne(0,0)$ be a point of this circle. Then $X^2+Y^2=\frac{r^2}dX$, so $X>0$. Its inversion is $\frac{r^2}{X^2+Y^2}(X,Y)=\frac{d}{X}(X,Y)=\left(d,\frac{dY}X\right)$, a point of $L$, and by Problem 4a inverting it returns $(X,Y)$. So every point of the circle except the origin is the image of a point of $L$. The origin is the center of inversion and is not attained.

**Answer: circle with center $\left(\frac{r^2}{2d},0\right)$, radius $\frac{r^2}{2d}$ (origin excluded)**

rmt-2005-power-08.title: Slice by parallel chords
rmt-2005-power-08.body:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of the minor arc $AB$ and $t_0=$ the distance from $C$ to line $AB$. The region is the union of the chords parallel to $AB$ at distances $t$ from $C$, $t_0\le t<r$, together with the point $M$ ($t=r$).

By Problem 7c (with a rotation) the inversion of the line at distance $t$ from $C$ is the circle through $C$ with diameter $\frac{r^2}t$ along the ray $CM$. The chord is the part of the line inside $\bigcirc C$, and points inside $\bigcirc C$ invert to points outside, so the chord inverts to the part of that circle lying outside $\bigcirc C$. For $t=t_0$ the circle passes through $A$ and $B$ (points of $\bigcirc C$ are fixed), so it is the circle $\Gamma$ through $C,A,B$. For $t=r$ the circle has diameter $CM$, lies inside $\bigcirc C$ and meets it only at $M$.

These circles are nested (all tangent at $C$ to the line perpendicular to $CM$), with diameters increasing from $r$ (at $t=r$) to $\frac{r^2}{t_0}$ (at $t=t_0$) and they fill the closed disk of $\Gamma$ minus the open disk with diameter $CM$. Every point outside $\bigcirc C$ lies outside the disk with diameter $CM$, so the union of their outer portions is exactly the set of points that are outside (or on) $\bigcirc C$ and inside (or on) $\Gamma$.

**Answer: that crescent-shaped region (the part of the disk bounded by circle $CAB$ lying outside $\bigcirc C$), boundaries included**

rmt-2005-power-09a.title: Orthogonality and power of a point
rmt-2005-power-09a.body:
Let the circle through $P$ be $\omega$ with center $O$ and radius $a$, orthogonal to $\bigcirc C$ at a point $X$. The tangents at $X$ are perpendicular, i.e. the radii $CX$ and $OX$ are perpendicular, so triangle $CXO$ has a right angle at $X$ and $OC^2=r^2+a^2$. Thus $C$ is outside $\omega$ and its power with respect to $\omega$ is $OC^2-a^2=r^2$.

The line $CP$ meets $\omega$ at $P$ and at a second point $K$ (possibly $K=P$ if tangent), and $CP\cdot CK=r^2$ (power of a point). Because $C$ is outside $\omega$, both intersection points are on the same side of $C$, i.e. $K$ is on ray $CP$. Then $K$ satisfies the defining conditions of the inversion, so $K=P'$ and $P'\in\omega$. ∎

rmt-2005-power-09b.title: Reverse the argument
rmt-2005-power-09b.body:
Let $\omega$ have center $O$ and radius $a$ and contain $P$ and $P'$ (distinct). The line $CP$ meets $\omega$ at exactly $P$ and $P'$, which are on the same side of $C$, so $C$ is outside $\omega$ and its power is $OC^2-a^2=CP\cdot CP'=r^2$. Hence $OC^2=r^2+a^2$.

Since $OC^2=r^2+a^2>(r-a)^2$ (for $r,a>0$) and $OC^2<(r+a)^2$ (as $2ra>0$), the circles intersect in two points $X$. At such a point $CX=r$, $OX=a$, and $CX^2+OX^2=OC^2$, so $\angle CXO=90^\circ$ by the converse of Pythagoras. The tangent to each circle at $X$ is perpendicular to its radius, so the tangents are perpendicular: the circles are orthogonal. ∎

rmt-2005-power-10.title: Use 9b
rmt-2005-power-10.body:
Let $\Gamma=\bigcirc C$ (radius $r$) and $\omega=\bigcirc D$, with $C\notin\omega$ (otherwise the inversion of $\omega$ is not defined). Since $\omega$ is mapped onto itself, for every $P\in\omega$ we have $P'\in\omega$.

*Case 1:* every $P\in\omega$ satisfies $P=P'$. By Problem 4b every point of $\omega$ lies on $\Gamma$, so $\omega\subseteq\Gamma$ and the two circles coincide.

*Case 2:* some $P\in\omega$ has $P\ne P'$. Then $\omega$ is a circle through $P$ and $P'$ with $P'\ne P$, so by Problem 9b it is orthogonal to $\Gamma$. ∎

rmt-2005-power-11a.title: Power of a point plus homothety
rmt-2005-power-11a.body:
For a point $P$ on $\bigcirc K$, let the line $CP$ meet $\bigcirc K$ again at $Q$ ($Q=P$ for a tangent line). Since $C$ is outside $\bigcirc K$, $P$ and $Q$ are on the same ray from $C$, and $CP\cdot CQ=w^2-a^2$ (power of $C$).

The inversion has $CP'=\frac{r^2}{CP}=\frac{r^2}{w^2-a^2}CQ$ on the same ray, i.e. $P'$ is the image of $Q$ under the homothety $h$ with center $C$ and ratio $\lambda=\frac{r^2}{w^2-a^2}$. As $P$ runs over $\bigcirc K$, $Q=\sigma(P)$ also runs over all of $\bigcirc K$ ($\sigma$ is an involution of the circle). Hence the inversion of $\bigcirc K$ is $h(\bigcirc K)$, a circle with center on line $CK$ (the image of $K$) and radius $\lambda a$. ∎

rmt-2005-power-11b.title: From the homothety
rmt-2005-power-11b.body:
By the proof of 11a, the image is a homothety of $\bigcirc K$ with ratio $\frac{r^2}{w^2-a^2}$, so its radius is $\frac{ar^2}{w^2-a^2}$.

(Check: the points of $\bigcirc K$ nearest and farthest from $C$ are at distances $w-a$ and $w+a$; they invert to distances $\frac{r^2}{w-a}$ and $\frac{r^2}{w+a}$, a diameter of length $\frac{r^2}{w-a}-\frac{r^2}{w+a}=\frac{2ar^2}{w^2-a^2}$.)

**Answer: $\frac{ar^2}{w^2-a^2}$**

rmt-2005-power-12.title: Similar triangles
rmt-2005-power-12.body:
Let $T$ be a point of $C_1$ near $P$, with inversions $T',P'$. From $OP\cdot OP'=OT\cdot OT'=r^2$ we get $\frac{OP}{OT}=\frac{OT'}{OP'}$, and the triangles $OPT$ and $OT'P'$ share the angle at $O$, so they are similar: $\angle OTP=\angle OP'T'$ and $\angle OPT=\angle OT'P'$.

Now let $T\to P$ along $C_1$. The line $PT$ tends to the tangent $t_1$ of $C_1$ at $P$, and $P'T'$ tends to the tangent $t_1'$ of the inverted curve at $P'$ (the inverted curve is a curve by assumption). So the angle between line $OP$ and $t_1$ at the point $P$ equals, in magnitude, the angle between $OP'$ (the same line $OP$) and $t_1'$ at $P'$; the triangle similarity reverses orientation, so $t_1'$ is the reflection of $t_1$ in the perpendicular bisector of $PP'$ (the reflection maps line $OP$ to itself).

The same applies to $C_2$: $t_2'$ is the reflection of $t_2$ in the same line. A reflection preserves the angle between two lines, so the angle between $t_1',t_2'$ equals the angle between $t_1,t_2$. ∎

rmt-2005-power-13a.title: Inversion at A
rmt-2005-power-13a.body:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Since $AB=AC$ and the rhombus $BQCP$ has $PB=PC$, $QB=QC$, the points $A,P,Q,M$ all lie on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, and $M$ is the midpoint of $PQ$ (diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other and are perpendicular). With $BM=h$: $PM=MQ=\sqrt{y^2-h^2}$ and $AM=\sqrt{x^2-h^2}>PM$. Taking $P$ as the vertex between $A$ and $M$ (as in the figure), $AP=AM-PM$, $AQ=AM+PM$, so
$$AP\cdot AQ=AM^2-PM^2=(x^2-h^2)-(y^2-h^2)=x^2-y^2=:k^2,$$
a constant independent of the shape of the linkage. Also $P$ and $Q$ are on the same ray from $A$. So $Q$ is the inversion of $P$ about the circle $\bigcirc A$ of radius $k=\sqrt{x^2-y^2}$.

Now choose any fixed point $Z\ne A$. The condition $PZ=AZ$ says that $P$ lies on the circle $\omega$ with center $Z$ passing through $A$. By Problems 7c and 4a (after translating/rotating coordinates so that $A$ is the origin and $Z$ lies on the $x$-axis), the inversion of a circle through the center of inversion (minus that center) is a line perpendicular to $AZ$, at distance $\frac{k^2}{2AZ}$ from $A$. Hence $Q$ lies on a line. Since the geometry of the linkage ($0<h\le y$) restricts $AP$ to the interval $[x-y,\,k]$ and $AQ$ to $[k,\,x+y]$, the point $P$ traverses only an arc of $\omega$ and so $Q$ traverses only a segment of that line. ∎
